name: regldg
desc: Regular expression grammar language dictionary generator
why: A generator that produces dictionaries from regex grammars, turning a pattern language into a word list in an odd way.

brief.what_it_is: regldg is a command-line program, written in C, that takes a regular expression pattern and generates every string of text that matches it. The output is a word list, so the program works as a dictionary generator. The homepage describes it as a "regular expression grammar language dictionary generator" and gives the current version as 1.0.1. It supports a subset of Perl's regex syntax, with some differences noted on the page.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wrote it to get a password list: he knew a password started with "omu" and was 7 characters long, and had only a very old computer. The page frames it as the reverse of normal regex use, where a pattern is used to test whether a string matches.
brief.how_it_works: You give regldg a pattern and it enumerates all the strings in the language that the pattern defines. The page describes regex as defining a grammar, and the words matching it as that grammar's language. The page does not describe the enumeration algorithm. It also says uniqueness is not guaranteed, so duplicates can appear, for example from a{2,3}a{3,2}.

commands_seen.context: Suggested on the homepage as a Perl regex tutorial to read on *nix systems. It is a man page lookup, not a regldg command.
Also suggested on the homepage as a Perl regex reference. The page appears to mean perlretut, since it names that section earlier. This is a man page lookup, not a regldg command.

brief.install_notes: The homepage says regldg is written in C and should run on any platform with a C compiler, but that it has not been tested beyond that. It gives no build steps, no configuration, and no first-run instructions. Nothing on the homepage mentions the Homebrew formula.
brief.standout: It inverts the usual regex direction: instead of testing strings against a pattern, it enumerates every string the pattern matches. The author also made deliberate syntax changes to avoid Perl ambiguities, such as using \o40, \x20, or \z32 for character codes so that \1 is always a backreference.
brief.status: The homepage shows version 1.0.1 and has no release date, changelog, or repository link. The maintenance state can't be determined from the homepage alone, so it is unknown.
brief.caveats: The homepage says the program "has not been tested" on platforms beyond its own, and it is not clear which systems were tested. Perl's named character classes such as {IsUpper} and [:digit:] are not implemented. Non-capturing groups and zero-width assertions are also missing. Patterns like a* can produce output the author does not know how to define, and the author deliberately left those unimplemented. No license is stated on the homepage.
quotes: regldg, as it says above, is a regular expression grammar language dictionary generator.
In regldg, you give it a pattern, and it will create all the strings of text which match it.
regldg is written in c, and should be able to be run (but has not been tested) on any platform which has a c compiler.
uniqueness in the output is not guaranteed.
fetch_log: https://regldg.com/ : fetched OK, returned the homepage text including the README-style description. The page names two docs pages (regular expressions capabilities; regular expressions differences between perl and regldg) but gives no URLs, so I did not follow them.

judge.reason: It turns regexes from filters into generators, making the idea of a pattern’s language tangible through an unusual, hands-on word-list tool.

entry.title: regldg
entry.tldr: Runs regular expressions backwards: give it a pattern and it prints every string that matches, turning a regex into a word list.
entry.deeper_look:
Most people use a regex to ask whether a string matches. regldg flips that. You hand it a pattern and it enumerates every string the pattern describes. The homepage puts it plainly: "In regldg, you give it a pattern, and it will create all the strings of text which match it."

The author wrote it to build a password list. He knew a password started with "omu" and was 7 characters long, and he had only a very old computer. A pattern that fixes the prefix and the length gives a small, finite list to try. That origin explains why it is a dictionary generator and not a general string toy.

The idea underneath is that a regex defines a grammar, and the words matching it are that grammar's language. Normally you only ever test membership in that language. Here you walk the whole thing. It is a quick way to feel how pattern size turns into output size, and why a pattern like a* is awkward: the language is infinite, and the author deliberately left such cases unimplemented.

It supports a subset of Perl's regex syntax, with deliberate changes to avoid ambiguity. Character codes are written as \o40, \x20, or \z32, so that \1 is always a backreference. The homepage says uniqueness in the output is not guaranteed, so duplicates can appear, for example from a{2,3}a{3,2}.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the program's usage text, so you can see how it takes a pattern.
Opens Perl's quick regex tutorial, which the homepage suggests for learning the pattern syntax regldg accepts a subset of.

entry.whats_unique: It inverts the usual regex direction, enumerating every string a pattern matches instead of testing one. The author also changed some Perl syntax on purpose to remove ambiguity.
entry.caveats: The homepage gives no release date or repository, so maintenance is unknown, and it lacks Perl's named character classes, non-capturing groups, and zero-width assertions.
